blindSummary:
This state/province operates a religious-law-derived criminal code, adopted by a twelve-state bloc of the country by 2002. Religious courts have jurisdiction over criminal matters for adherents of the state religion, and the penal code extends criminalisation to same-sex acts between women. No trans-specific incident or documented religious morality-police enforcement appears for this state/province in this dossier. The legal architecture adds a parallel criminal-jurisdiction layer absent in the country's civil-law states.

Assessed risk here sits slightly below the country-wide average, alongside the group of bloc states that share the enacted system without case-level documentation of it being applied to trans people. The enacted system itself is what distinguishes this state/province; the absence of enforcement or incident documentation — unlike several sibling bloc states examined in a foreign faith-liberty commission's country study — prevents a deeper assessment. By contrast, the federal capital territory, which has no religious criminal jurisdiction, has a documented killing of a trans person and a state-implicated failure to investigate.
